newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - French audit risks upset to EMU plays.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - French audit risks upset to EMU plays.

text.p: France must act quickly to plug gaps in its budget or risk throwing convergence plays into disarray, and incurring Germany's wrath, analysts said on Friday.

On Monday, France's audit of public finances is expected to show the 1997 deficit will stand at 3.5 to 3.6 percent of gross domestic product -- in excess of the 3.0 percent designated by the Maastricht currency convergence criteria.

"There's a potential risk from an EMU (European Economic and Monetary Union) perspective," said Ken Wattret, international economist at Paribas Capital Markets in London. "It's important for France to roll out a series of measures very quickly or there's going to be an adverse reaction in the southern European states."
He said the spread between 10-year Italian BTP yields and comparable German Bunds could widen back above the 100 basis point level, from a current level of 94 basis points.

But analysts said French bond investors were only likely to be moved from their policy of holding onto OATs and hoping for the best if a 1997 deficit to GDP ratio of 3.8 percent or more were announced.

"You could get a narrowing of the spread from the current minus 13 to below minus 10," said Gwyn Hacche, international economist at HSBC James Capel. "There would also be a geared effect on countries like Italy."
Analysts said the speed and severity of France's actions are likely to be influenced by how it considers Germany will view the failure to meet the convergence criteria.

"At the moment Germany is just slapping wrists over individual countries' shortcomings, not threatening a delay to EMU," said Wattret. "But if they start talking tough it's going to have a knock on effect on convergence plays," said Wattret.
A reduction of 0.3 percentage points from the 3.6 percent of GDP to the 3.3 percent target expected would require extra revenues or spending cuts of around 25 billion francs.

But any "quick fix" solutions, such as one-off rises in corporate tax, could resurrect concerns that monetary union is only going ahead based on creative accounting, rather than sustainable economic prudence, analysts said.

"A corporation tax surcharge could yield 10 to 12 billion francs, but the big issue is sustainability," said Hacche. "Another of the one-off measures, France Telecom, drops out next year, so that will also have to be accounted for."
The 1998 budget, which the audit may also comment on, will lack the previous budget's transfer of funds from France Telecom, which was worth 37.5 billion francs or 0.45 percent of GDP.

"The 1998 number (deficit to GDP) is crucial," said Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Markets in London. "There are fears that it could be 4.0 percent, and the socialists' aim of no more austerity is certainly at odds with the stability pact."
A French government spokeswoman said on Thursday that the government will not impose a new austerity plan just to meet a stricht interpretation of the Maastricht treaty.
But Roberts said French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn and Prime Minister Lionel Jospin appeared to be preparing the ground for such a change of heart.
Wattret said the government's solution to a "ballooning 1998 deficit" might be to emphasise the fact that this is a problem inherited from the last government, and promise to address it.
